notes:
Supersedes impl/positional-index/positional-varint in place: same file, same statement, same reader
interface, one format version higher (B2SI v3, and v2 is now refused rather than misread — index/ is
scratch, a stale index must say "re-index"). Nothing about WHAT the index answers changed; this is
the encoding, and it is 31.6% smaller: 34 224 -> 23 403 bytes, 0.3727 -> 0.2548 of the corpus.

Where the bytes went, section by section (sample-docs.jsonl, 120 docs, 560 terms, 10 753 postings,
13 973 occurrences):
  postings         27 240 -> 18 856    binary interpolative coding
  term dictionary   2 953 ->  3 110    front-coded, and it now carries the posting-list lengths
  term/post offsets 2 244 ->    144    one entry per 16 terms instead of one per term
  document ids      1 172 ->    698    the same front-coded table, addressed by position
  header              299 ->    279    format and version live in the 9-byte prefix, not twice

BIC is the whole story. A term's document list is a sorted subset of [0, docCount) and its positions
inside a document are a sorted subset of [0, span): code the middle element against the tightest
range its rank allows (truncated binary), then recurse into the two ranges it just split. A stretch
that fills its range exactly costs literally zero bits. That charges for how CLUSTERED a list is,
which is the actual shape of postings, and it removes gaps, continuation bits and byte alignment in
one move. Measured against the information-theoretic bound (sum of log2 C(universe, size) over every
list) of 16 161 bytes, this lands at 18 856 — the remaining overhead is the df varints, the repeat
coding and one byte-alignment per term, all of which buy per-term random access.

Two encoding choices worth not re-deriving:
  - tf is NOT stored per posting. Which postings repeat is a sparse subset of the list, coded as
    tb(count) + BIC of the slots, then gamma(tf-1) for each. 9 174 of 10 753 postings here hold a
    single occurrence, so a per-posting count is almost all zeros. (The v2 trick — folding "tf is 1"
    into the low bit of the document gap — has no equivalent once gaps are gone; this replaces it and
    costs about the same 1 500 bytes.)
  - the position universe is the document's span (titleLen + 1 + bodyLen), read off the two length
    sections. That is why titleLen is persisted, and it is also what keeps the title/body split
    derivable from the positions alone.

Dead ends, measured on this corpus before choosing BIC: a per-posting-list fixed bit width (frame of
reference) gave 23 301 bytes and blocks of 32 gave 23 193 — barely a sixth of BIC's win, because the
widest value in a list sets the price for all of them. Elias gamma over the v2 value stream was
WORSE than the v2 varints (28 388). A raw single/multi bitmap instead of the BIC'd repeat subset
costs 464 bytes more. Front coding without blocks saves another ~100 bytes but loses binary search.

Reader cost was measured, not assumed. Decoding is ~0.6 ms slower cold than v2's varints (more code
to JIT on a path that runs once), and three things pay that back and more: postings are memoised per
process (a phrase query asks phrase-matching and bm25-ranking for the same terms), varint decoding
returns its cursor out-of-band instead of allocating a [value, pos] tuple per integer, and a
dictionary block scan compares in one reusable key buffer instead of concatenating a Buffer per term.
Both readers also now refuse to spin: a varint or bit stream that runs past the end of the file
throws instead of looping forever on undefined bytes (a mutant found that — bench/mutate.mjs left two
runaway test processes behind before the guard existed).

Five mutants in bench/mutate.mjs pin the new mechanisms: position universe off by one, repeat counts
off by one, front-coded entries not trimmed, the shared prefix dropped on read, and block-skip
offsets that stop counting posting lengths. All five go red on this contract's own gate, which still
runs the deprecated inverted-index gate alongside the positional one.
